detail.abstract: The global subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market has grown rapidly, yet platforms increasingly compete on near-identical offerings, and signs of subscriber fatigue have emerged. This working paper examines service integration, meaning the association of complementary non-content services with a platform's offering, as a strategy for functional differentiation in a saturated market. It draws on publicly available industry and public-health data and on platform economics literature, and presents Madi Fast, a patented concept developed by Mason Ewing Corporation for the Madison Channel platform, as an illustrative case. The paper situates the concept within the SVOD competitive landscape, discusses accessibility for people with visual impairments or reduced mobility as a core design principle, and identifies directions for empirical research. Technical implementation details are protected by a patent filed with the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) and are not disclosed.

title: Persona-Conditioned Generative Agents as a Method for Studying Online Communities

detail.title: Persona-Conditioned Generative Agents as a Method for Studying Online Communities

declarations.funderStatement: Wisconsin School of Business

detail.abstract: Online discussions on digital platforms reflect only one realized conversational trajectory, shaped by who chooses to participate and how participants interact. This makes it difficult to know how the same discussion might have evolved under a different participant mix, because changing who participates can also change what subsequent participants see and say. We develop a GenAI-enabled agent-based simulation method for constructing these otherwise unobservable counterfactual conversations and benchmarking them against observed human discussion. The method constructs persona-conditioned agents from empirically observed linguistic and demographic profiles, allows agents to interact sequentially within the same discussion context and also varies participant composition to test whether discussion breadth and topics change as a result. We apply the framework to Reddit discussions across four domains (Entertainment, Games, People/Relationships and Technology), and compare generic AI and persona-conditioned AI simulations with observed human conversations. We find that while persona-AI generate content that is significantly closer to human discussions (in terms of metrics like length, first-person language, semantic diversity and sentiment) relative to generic AI, the semantic breadth of discussions remains narrow and more positive in tone than human discussion. Increasing the sampling probability of users underrepresented in the human data partially changes which topics are discussed, but does not broadly increase conversational breadth or reproduce the diversity of human discourse. These findings illustrate that persona conditioning can be a powerful tool to generate otherwise unobservable counterfactual conversations, and identify scenarios where additional validation is required before drawing conclusions about human behavior.

title: Scalable Agricultural Intelligence: AI as an Input to Agricultural Production

detail.title: Scalable Agricultural Intelligence: AI as an Input to Agricultural Production

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence in agriculture is often described as a substitute for labor or as a tool for improving prediction, precision, and control. Yet many agricultural systems are constrained by a different scarce resource: experienced judgment. A farm may have land, capital, equipment, workers, and demand, but still depend on a limited number of people who know what to notice, how to interpret changing conditions, and when to intervene. This paper develops the Scalable Agricultural Intelligence framework by formalizing the argument in Kao (2026a) that intelligence can be treated as an agricultural input alongside more visible inputs such as land, labor, water, energy, and capital. The term does not imply a standardized factor of production. It identifies the operational capacity to observe conditions, interpret their significance, and select useful actions.

The paper connects agricultural extension, decision-support systems, human-centered AI, agricultural expertise, and the economics of knowledge in organizations. It introduces four definitions: Agricultural Intelligence, Judgment Bottleneck, Expertise Reach, and Scalable Agricultural Intelligence. The central mechanism is that AI can reduce the amount of routine expert judgment required per unit of production, route exceptional cases toward scarce experts, lower the knowledge required at the point of entry for less experienced operators, and partially separate expertise from physical location. A lightweight formulation expresses expertise reach as a capacity relationship rather than a calibrated production function.

Evidence from digital agricultural extension, autonomous greenhouse experiments, human-centered agricultural AI, and recent workplace AI research supports components of this mechanism while also showing its limits. Digital advice can expand knowledge reach without automatically raising output; agricultural skill contains embodied and contextual elements that are not readily codified; and AI benefits may be largest where routine decisions can be supported while humans retain responsibility for unusual conditions. The paper therefore argues that AI need not replace agricultural experts to change agricultural economics. It may be sufficient for the same

title: Agentic AI as a Cognitive Partner

detail.title: Agentic AI as a Cognitive Partner

detail.abstract: Education was already under pressure to move beyond knowledge transmission toward the development of transferable human capabilities before generative AI arrived. AI makes this transition more urgent because it can produce many of the artifacts traditionally used as proxies for learning. The same technology also creates an opportunity: carefully designed agents can make individualized questioning, challenge, feedback, reflection and practice available more frequently and at greater scale than conventional teaching economics allow. This paper is a call to action for educational design. It asks what learners should become more capable of doing, which experiences develop those capabilities, what work AI should remove once its marginal learning value is low, and what consequential thinking, interaction and judgement should remain with the learner. Innovation Cartography provides the worked example through three simultaneous layers of learning: process discipline, an authentic innovation journey, and transferable capability development. Agents can support individual and team learning across all three layers. Evidence of development should include how learners question, listen, communicate, collaborate, interpret evidence, respond to feedback and exercise judgement over time. Progress should not be defined by declining AI use; more capable learners may use AI more deeply and deliberately. The opportunity is to improve human-AI collaboration, redirect time from alreadymastered work toward the next learning frontier, make strong pedagogical practices shareable, and use deployment evidence to improve both learning and pedagogy.

title: A Review and Forecast of Student Enrolment in Malaysian Higher Education Institutions, 2000–2025

detail.title: A Review and Forecast of Student Enrolment in Malaysian Higher Education Institutions, 2000–2025

detail.abstract: This paper reviews the evolution of student enrolment across Malaysian higher education institutions (HEIs) between 2000 and 2025 and develops forward-looking projections to 2040 using three complementary quantitative approaches. Drawing on an integrated dataset covering public universities, teacher education institutes, polytechnics, and private HEIs, the analysis documents a total-enrolment expansion from 325,741 students in 2000 to a peak of 1,342,278 in 2016, followed by a contraction to 1,202,202 in 2022 and a partial recovery to 1,367,929 by 2025 (compound annual growth rate of 5.9% over the full period). Engineering, Manufacturing and Construction (EMC) enrolment-a policy-priority field-peaked at 300,150 students in 2018 before declining by approximately 25% to 224,089 in 2025, and its share of total enrolment fell from a high of 22.6% (2010) to 16.4% (2025). International student enrolment, by contrast, grew steadily to a record 159,138 in 2025 (11.6% of total enrolment). Chow structural-break tests confirm statistically significant regime changes around 2016 (p < 0.001) and 2022 (p = 0.002), consistent with a post-2016 plateau/decline and a post-2022 recovery. A damped Holt exponential-smoothing model projects EMC enrolment to continue declining moderately to approximately 197,000 by 2030. For total enrolment, a logistic (saturation) trend model-which best fits the historical data-projects growth to roughly 1.64 million by 2035, while an independent demographic model driven by Malaysia's already-born 18-24 cohort and a rising participationrate assumption projects a broadly similar trajectory that peaks near 1.65 million around 2036 before declining as the cohort itself shrinks. The convergence and eventual divergence of these two independently derived forecasts is discussed as evidence for, and a boundary condition on, continued enrolment growth. The paper concludes with implications for capacity planning, field-of-study policy (particularly the STEM/EMC pipeline), and internationalisation strategy in the Malaysian higher education sector.

detail.abstract: This systematic qualitative study synthesizes findings from 43 peer-reviewed articles, policy papers and practitioner reports from 2004 to 2026 to examine the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) and blockchain technologies on last‑mile delivery in Africa. Using a structured thematic synthesis, the paper reviewed evidence across three outcome domains- operational efficiency, sustainability, and customer satisfaction and identified cross‑cutting challenges and technology‑enabled solutions specific to the African last‑mile context. Findings indicate that Artificial Intelligence (AI) (route optimization, demand forecasting, dynamic dispatching, and predictive maintenance) substantially improves operational efficiency by reducing travel distances, lowering idle times, and increasing vehicle utilization; however, benefits are uneven due to data scarcity, poor geospatial infrastructure, and limited technical capacity. Blockchain applications (smart contracts, provenance tracking, and decentralized payment settlements) enhance transparency, trust and secure information flows among fragmented stakeholders, addressing payment delays and fraud risks endemic to many markets. Together, AI and blockchain create synergistic value - AI generates actionable, real‑time insights while blockchain ensures immutable, auditable transaction records - facilitating reliable peer‑to‑peer courier networks and interoperable multi‑actor platforms. Sustainability gains emerge through emissions reductions from optimized routing and modal integration, though constrained by legacy fleet composition and weak regulatory incentives. Customer satisfaction improves when technologies enable accurate Estimated Time of Arrivals (ETAs), proof‑of‑delivery and dispute resolution, but adoption is hampered by limited digital literacy, device penetration and concerns around data privacy. We conclude with a framework of practical enablers- data governance, public–private partnerships, capacity building, and adaptable regulatory regimes and recommend research on scalable pilot interventions, cost‑benefit analyses in low‑resource settings, and human‑centred design approaches to ensure equitable, sustainable deployment of AI and blockchain in Africa’s last mile.

title: Stop Polling, Start Observing: The Experience Entropy Index (EEI) as a Passive Framework for Measuring Customer Journey Friction

detail.title: Stop Polling, Start Observing: The Experience Entropy Index (EEI) as a Passive Framework for Measuring Customer Journey Friction

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. This framework was developed independently in a personal capacity.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Most organizations today measure customer experience (CX) using frameworks like the Net Promoter Score (NPS) and Customer Satisfaction (CSAT). However, these methods rely on active post-interaction surveys, forcing the customer to do the analytical work of grading internal business processes. Furthermore, standard customer surveys suffer from severe non-response bias. With standard digital outreach often capturing median response rates hovering between 10% and 15%, organizations capture only the vocal extremes of the highly satisfied or highly frustrated, completely missing the "silent middle" majority. This paper introduces the Experience Entropy Index (EEI), a passive measurement framework that quantifies systemic friction and cognitive load without asking the customer a single question. Borrowing the concept of entropy from physics as a measure of chaos, EEI evaluates customer journeys using three passive system variables: the Loopback Coefficient (operational loopbacks), Resolution Latency (dead time), and Unprompted Sentiment Shift (emotional degradation measured via analytics). Calculated on a normalized 0 to 100 scale, EEI offers a survey-less methodology with a 100% capture rate. By minimizing entropy, organizations can transition from delivering sporadic moments of delight to delivering a highly consistent, predictable, and surprise-free customer experience.

detail.abstract: This paper synthesises the existing research on the dynamics of innovation diffusion, with a focus on Bass-type models and their extensions. The theoretical foundation of innovation diffusion proposed by Rogers (1962) and the seminal work of Bass (1969) serve as a starting point for the analysis. We identify and examine various generalizations and stochastic extensions of the Bass model, including counting processes, diffusion processes, and uncertain processes, as well as parameter estimation techniques, from classical statistical techniques to more advanced techniques such as Bayesian filtering and metaheuristic optimisation. We finally explore alternative models of innovation diffusion, with a particular focus on agent-based models. This overview of the evolution of Bass-type models illustrates the progress made in innovation diffusion research over the past decades.

detail.abstract: This paper documents a new form of state dependence in international monetary transmission: with higher fiscal-policy uncertainty, the relative importance of current-rate and future-rate/path U.S. monetary news changes as transmission unfolds. Using high-frequency FOMC surprises and state-dependent local projections conditioned on lagged globally salient fiscal-policy uncertainty, I find a pronounced short-to-medium rotation in credit-risk pricing towards current-rate news. Between months 0-3 and 9-12, the current-minus-future fiscal-state sensitivity rises by about 69.7 basis points for EMBI sovereign spreads and 0.42 percentage points for the U.S. excess bond premium. The rotation is concentrated in current-rate sensitivity, while the future-rate component is small and imprecisely estimated. A one-dimensional monetary-news measure reveals no comparable rotation, suggesting that scalar aggregation can conceal economically important state-dependent reweighting.

detail.abstract: Public dissatisfaction with democratic institutions is often discussed as a crisis of democracy. This framing risks conflating democracy with one historically contingent implementation of it: electoral representation by professional politicians organised through competitive political careers. Separating the democratic principlepopular control under conditions of political equality-from the mechanisms used to realise it, this paper treats elections, parties and political careers as design choices. It develops a constitutional alternative: a citizen legislature selected by civic lottery, with fixed non-renewable terms and structured access to competing expertise. The claim is institutional: change the selection function, and many of the biases and career incentives that competitive political careers build into the legislature go with it.

title: The Human Virus Paradox: Human Expansion, Ecological Limits and the Legal Foundations of Environmental Responsibility

detail.title: The Human Virus Paradox: Human Expansion, Ecological Limits and the Legal Foundations of Environmental Responsibility

detail.abstract: Organic-disease metaphors for human expansion, in which humanity figures as a virus, a parasite or a cancer on the biosphere, are common in environmental discourse. This article asks whether that species-level diagnosis can carry legal weight, and how ecological limits enter law without collapsing responsibility into collective guilt. It applies doctrinal, comparative and interpretive analysis to international instruments, international and regional judicial decisions, and constitutional adjudication in Germany, the Netherlands, Brazil and Colombia, and reads scientific assessments of planetary boundaries, population projections and emissions inequality as evidence about the factual predicates of legal duties. The article identifies a paradox internal to the metaphor: the capacity for foresight and self-restraint that makes human expansion ecologically distinctive is the capacity that makes legal responsibility possible, and a virus, by definition, lacks it. The article contends that ecological science performs three distinct functions in law, diagnostic, attributive and calibrative, and that courts and legislators have used it chiefly in the calibrative function, to set the stringency of duties borne by identifiable duty-bearers rather than to assign guilt to a species. On this reading the International Court of Justice's 2025 climate advisory opinion, Urgenda, Neubauer, KlimaSeniorinnen and Brazil's ADPF 708 are variations on one structure. The article confronts the cornucopian and ecocentric objections, states conditions under which its thesis would fail, and derives an interpretive proposition on limit-informed due diligence. Its conclusions are doctrinal and interpretive, not empirical. detail.abstract: An expression of concern (EoC) is meant to alert readers and potential citers of a scientific paper that there may be ethical or other integrity-related issues associated with that paper. Despite this, there are EoCs that lack insufficient details regarding their background, thus not serving as effective scientific communication tools. In this article, which is an extended descriptive observation and not an empirical research study, a batch of 42 EoCs published between 1 January 2022 and 18 May 2024, as indexed at the Retraction Watch database, were initially assessed on 20 May 2024. Of these, 13 papers had been retracted after the EoC had been issued whereas the remaining 29 cases still had an EoC associated with them, and remained unresolved, spanning between 450 days old (25 July 2023) and 811 days old (3 March 2022). A reassessment on 23 December 2024 revealed that two more EoCs had been resolved, i.e., 15 papers had been retracted, and from the remaining 27 unresolved cases, the ages of the EoCs ranged between 667 days old (27 February 2023) and 1028 days old (3 March 2022). A second reassessment on 29 October 2025 revealed that none of the remaining 27 unresolved cases had yet been resolved. A third reassessment on 8 July 2026 revealed that nine more cases had been resolved, but the unresolved cases now span from 1228 days old (27 February 2023) and 1589 days old (3 March 2022). Gaining an understanding of the content and background of EoCs might offer additional insight into why such papers have not yet been retracted. This exercise also offers a unique focus on a batch of 42 EoCs, showing how their status evolved over a more than two-year period, opening a field of research dedicated to this unique corrective measure and precursor to retractions.

detail.abstract: Persistent historical dollarisation does not fully summarise the currency-state information relevant for uncertainty transmission: conditional on a historical benchmark, the prevailing currency configuration contains additional information about real responses. Across 103 economies, conditioning country uncertainty on observable international information yields an internationally unspanned innovation with more adverse GDP and consumption responses at higher predetermined deposit dollarisation. The inherited deposit share is decomposed into historical exposure and the prevailing state. At two years, a ten-percentage-point higher prevailing state is associated with GDP and consumption gradients of about-0.57 and-0.66 percentage points, versus-0.09 and-0.27 for historical exposure. Preferred year-cluster inference detects the prevailing-state gradients, which remain negative when the measurement stage is re-estimated; direct state-history comparisons are less precise. A structural framework rationalises the distinction through household currency insurance, incomplete currency transformation and slow-moving financial accommodation.

title: Organizational Precedents and Value Preservation in AI Cost Reduction Decisions

detail.title: Organizational Precedents and Value Preservation in AI Cost Reduction Decisions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: ML, DL, LLM, business management, Financial economics

detail.abstract: Firms increasingly ask AI assistants to help choose which cost reduction initiatives to fund, and they often supply past approval records as context. If past decisions systematically left value unrealized, an assistant that learns from or defers to those precedents may reproduce the loss. We study this risk in two steps. Study 1 uses 49,881 energy efficiency recommendations made to 8,547 U.S. manufacturing plants by the Industrial Training and Assessment Centers between 2005 and 2023, analysed under a plan fixed before outcomes were examined and confirmed once on a 70% holdout of plants. Among recommendations with positive net present value at a 10% rate and a five-year life, 59.7% of the value (95% plant-cluster interval 57.2-62.2%) was not implemented, and the unimplemented share rose with payback period and project size. Within plants, implementation responded strongly to upfront cost but not detectably to annual savings. Holding each plant's own spending fixed, its actual choices forwent 24.4% of the achievable value range; a model trained on past implementation decisions forwent 14.3%, whereas a simple shortest-payback rule forwent 6.6%. Learning from precedent therefore inherits a large part of the value left behind. Study 2 is a randomized experiment in which frozen language models select initiative portfolios from real recommendations under a stated net-present-value objective, while matched synthetic histories vary the share of past approvals that favoured headline savings over net value. Its inputs, prompts and analysis plan were locked before any model call, and its results will be reported in a revised version. Together the studies connect organizational precedent to a measurable opportunity cost and suggest checking AI recommendations against an explicit economic ledger rather than against past approvals. Keywords: cost reduction; capital budgeting; energy efficiency gap; large language models; organizational precedents; decision support

detail.abstract: This paper examines competition law and policy in Kenya and Africa, focusing on the regulation of markets, restrictive trade practices, abuse of market power, and mergers to support structural transformation. It traces the evolution of Kenyan competition law from the 1988 Restrictive Trade Practices, Monopolies and Price Control Act to the Competition Act 2010 and subsequent amendments, including reforms on abuse of buyer power and proposed digital-market provisions. The analysis covers institutional arrangements under the Competition Authority of Kenya and the Competition Tribunal, substantive rules on cartels, vertical restraints, dominance, and merger control, as well as consumer protection. The paper concludes by proposing legislative, institutional, and regional reforms to indigenize competition policy for Kenya’s dualistic, digitizing economy.

title: Governing the Intangible: Philippine Policy Options for Semiconductor and Electronics Design, Intellectual Property Protection, and Strategic-Trade Compliance

detail.title: Governing the Intangible: Philippine Policy Options for Semiconductor and Electronics Design, Intellectual Property Protection, and Strategic-Trade Compliance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: Pacific Forum is acknowledged.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Pacific Forum Issues & Insights, Volume 26, No. 13, pp. 186-209

detail.abstract:
The Philippines has built one of the largest semiconductor and electronics manufacturing bases in the Indo-Pacific, but most of that strength is in assembly, test and packaging (ATP), not chip design. As the country attempts to move up the value chain into design, research and development (R&D), and fabless innovation, it is confronted with a governance problem that traditional intellectual property (IP) policy was not designed to address. Semiconductor design work is no longer contained within a single company or jurisdiction; it is present in foreign electronic design automation (EDA) software, foundry-supplied process design kits (PDKs), cloud platforms, shared code repositories, and collaborators spread across the globe. The most valuable assets, such as design files, licensing terms, foundry data, and know-how, are intangible, moving by keystroke rather than by shipment, and need governance of access, licensing, and digital infrastructure, not just patents. 

This paper draws on a qualitative policy research design combining doctrinal and institutional analysis, comparative benchmarking of Taiwan, Singapore, South Korea, Japan, and the Philippines, five case studies of legal disputes and shared-infrastructure models, documentary evidence from a Luzon Economic Corridor infrastructure-financing event, and a Pacific Forum discussion on artificial intelligence (AI) compute and export controls. It also is informed by interviews with Philippine and international stakeholders, including an open-source IC design researcher, engineering deans and program leaders at three universities, officials of the Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines (IPOPHL), the Board of Investments (BOI), a Taiwanese university comparator, the president of the Philippine Integrated Circuit Design Association (PICDA), and a government-affairs executive at a leading global semiconductor manufacturer.

Four findings are presented. First, semiconductor design governance is a stack issue, not a single-instrument issue: design projects carry overlapping rights and restrictions across the EDA tool license, the design itself, PDK and foundry data, third-party IP, the infrastructure that carries the work, and the people allowed to touch it. Treating one layer as the whole picture leaves the others exposed. 

Second, access is now a governance event in itself. A student logging into a shared repository, running a cloud build, or opening a remote desktop session can move or expose sensitive technical information without a formal export or file transfer. Philippine institutional practice, including university IP policy, still largely assumes technology transfer as a shipment or signed license, not as a login. 

Third, the Philippine legal and institutional base is real. It is also incomplete. The IP Code protects local licensees but is structured for inbound licensing and does not itself prohibit outbound or controlled technology transfer. The country's IC layout design statute may not yet be operationalized for a true manufacturable chip layout. Trade secrets are lightly regulated in practice but are technically protected by law. Taiwan, Singapore, South Korea, and Japan have sophisticated semiconductor regimes that blend patents, special protection for IC layouts or "mask works", trade-secret regimes and, in the case of Taiwan and South Korea, extra safeguards for strategically sensitive technologies. No single instrument does the job, and the Philippines should not expect one to. 

Fourth, capability building and compliance readiness should be developed in parallel, not sequentially. The experience of universities such as the Mindanao State University-Iligan Institute of Technology (MSU-IIT) shows the feasibility of building credible IC-design capability in the regional universities, but only if research governance, IP management, and controlled EDA/PDK access mature together with the technical training. International comparators suggest a phased approach-attract investment and talent first and deepen compliance as projects become more sensitive rather than imposing heavy controls before there is an ecosystem to protect. An operating Philippine IC design firm confirms this on the demand side: the binding 186 constraint is the rate at which the ecosystem can produce qualified engineers, and overly rigid compliance risks widening, rather than closing, that capability gap.

title: When Is an Innovation Ready for Adoption? Behavioural Thresholds, Stakeholder Decisions and Evidence for Adoption Readiness

detail.title: When Is an Innovation Ready for Adoption? Behavioural Thresholds, Stakeholder Decisions and Evidence for Adoption Readiness

declarations.ethicsApproval: none
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: Innovation development is commonly organized around the progressive reduction of technical uncertainty. Technology Readiness Levels provide a useful language for identifying what must be learned or demonstrated before a technology can be relied upon in increasingly demanding settings. Yet the uncertainties that determine whether an innovation will be adopted are not solely technical. Adoption is a behavioural decision under uncertainty, and the proposed innovation competes not only with alternative solutions but with the privileged alternative of doing nothing. Consequential stakeholders must become sufficiently motivated and able to change behaviour: to test, approve, fund, insure, regulate, integrate, purchase, use, support or sustain an innovation. This paper develops Adoption Readiness as a complementary, evidencebased construct concerned with reducing uncertainty about those behavioural changes. It proposes that adoption is multi-stakeholder and threshold-based: each consequential stakeholder considers a different combination of conditions, and adoption progresses when the necessary stakeholders can and will cross the behavioural thresholds required along a particular adoption pathway. Behavioural economics and decision research help explain why apparently attractive innovations can remain stationary: reference dependence, loss aversion, status quo bias, habit, switching costs and organizational resistance privilege the current state. A Newtonian analogy, expressed as three Laws of Innovation Inertia, is introduced as a heuristic for making these forces visible: established behaviour tends to persist; greater organizational mass requires greater force to change at a given rate; and attempts at consequential change reveal countervailing forces. A six-box Adoption Journey Matrix diagnoses the forces supporting and inhibiting movement from current reality, through transition, to a future state, while readiness increases as assumptions are replaced by increasingly consequential behavioural evidence. First-user adoption is treated as a deliberate focal boundary because it creates a bounded zero-to-one behavioural outcome, not because the wider adoption journey ends there. Evidence and enabling actions developed during the firstuser journey may also shape subsequent use, broader adoption and long-lead conditions such as regulation. Adoption Readiness is therefore conceptualized not as the absence of commercialization barriers, but as the maturity of evidence that the consequential stakeholder behaviours required for a particular adoption episode can and will occur. detail.abstract: The international system of the twenty-first century is increasingly characterized by a condition of polycrisis in which armed conflicts, climate change, pandemics, forced migration, economic vulnerabilities, energy and food insecurity, digital transformation, and geopolitical competition interact rather than operate as isolated threats. This article examines a structural problem underlying these interconnected crises: the Global Solution Capacity Gap (GSCG). The central argument is that the capacity of the international system to generate, transmit, and amplify problems has expanded faster than its capacity to coordinate and implement collective solutions. As the geographical scope, interdependence, velocity, and complexity of global problems increase, institutional capacities for coordination, resource mobilization, implementation, and accountability do not necessarily expand at the same pace. The article integrates Robert W. Cox’s historical-structural approach, collective action theory, the global public goods literature, Elinor Ostrom’s polycentric governance perspective, scholarship on institutional fragmentation and regime complexity, and the human security approach. The article’s principal contribution is the development of a conceptual framework that defines the Global Solution Capacity Gap as the normalized difference between the demand for global problem-solving and the available solution capacity. It further proposes a five-dimensional Global Solution Capacity Index (GSCI) consisting of institutional coordination, crisis response capacity, implementation and compliance capacity, resource mobilization, and human security outcomes. The framework distinguishes institutional plurality from institutional incapacity. A plurality of institutions does not necessarily undermine governance; the critical issue is whether institutional interactions generate effective collective outcomes. The article therefore proposes that the central governance challenge of the twenty-first century is not simply the multiplication of crises but the widening distance between the systemic demand generated by interconnected global problems and the capacity of international institutions and actors to produce coordinated solutions.

detail.abstract:
Mens rea lies at the heart of the criminal law. It limits both who we punish — only the blameworthy, not the morally innocent — and how severely we punish them. In the United States, mens rea policy is driven by the Model Penal Code’s mens rea hierarchy (MPC hierarchy), which bases criminal liability and punishment on subtle differences in risk awareness — knowledge, recklessness, and negligence. But does U.S. mens rea policy reflect the views of the public? This Article reports results from the first nationally representative effort to answer this question. Our analysis of more than 6,000 survey responses offers the most detailed and statistically rigorous accounting to date of what the public thinks about mens rea.

Our study reveals that public attitudes broadly reflect some aspects of current mens rea policy, conflict with others, and are more complex than criminal policymakers and scholars previously thought. Departing from the landmark study in our field, we find that the public punishes in ways that broadly align with the MPC hierarchy. But we also find that some mens rea distinctions have a comparatively greater impact on how people punish certain types of crime, and that subtle differences in offense structure can influence public mens rea decisions in complex ways. These and other surprising patterns of punishment contradict long-held scholarly assumptions about the universality of criminal law norms. 

This new understanding of public attitudes has important implications for both criminal law and moral psychology. For policymakers and reformers, our study suggests that criminal punishment should more proportionately track differences in mens rea and illustrates how research on public attitudes might be used to lower sentences. For social scientists and criminal theorists, our study offers a more nuanced picture of lay moral judgment and uncovers unexpected ethical sensitivity in public punishment decisions. Our study also demonstrates the value of methodological refinement in experimental mens rea research, including the use of statistically representative participant pools and more realistic survey design.  All told, our study reveals how a more rigorous examination of public attitudes on mens rea can improve criminal policymaking and social science.

detail.abstract: Analysts routinely report single-point subjective probabilities, yet such reports conceal how much of the belief is evidence-backed, heuristic, or genuinely unknown. Classical fusion methods either presuppose coherence and independence, require an external base rate, or treat inputs atomically, leaving the internal structure of the belief being fused invisible. We introduce DSP-C (Dimensional-Shift Probability), a novel decomposition-and-calibration framework over reported subjective beliefs, whose fusion core re-parameterizes rather than replaces classical fusion. DSP-C decomposes each belief B and its complement NB into four components-Disbelief D, Unknown U , Evidence E, and Likelihood L (DUEL)-via a dimensional shift onto the belief-non-belief difference, and reconstructs a bias-corrected probability r(P) that mitigates over-and underconfidence while preserving boundedness. Reconstructed beliefs are fused through a triple-fusion pipeline that separately aggregates by Unknown and by Evidence and then blends the channels in log-odds space; the Dual-Uncertainty Reconstruction Operator (DURO) separates evidencelimited from analyst-side uncertainty. Appendix A shows that, under standard independence assumptions, DUEL pairwise fusion recovers the Bayes-odds product form (unit prior odds by default; optional base-rate anchor) and matches categorical Dempster-Shafer combination in the corresponding special case; the operational fusion, reconstruction, and recursive calibration layers, in contrast, are non-Bayesian. Recursive calibration layers (C 2-C 4) provide successive correction and stabilization; the sequence is realized in closed form by the bounded crissXcross equilibrium estimator r(P) x , whose boundedness and mean-sandwich properties are proven unconditionally in Appendix B.  On a 48-event synthetic stress suite spanning overconfident, herding, deceptive, and polarized regimes, and in comparative stress-tests against Subjective Logic and classical baselines, DSP-C variants substantially reduce Brier error in contested environments while preserving stability. Furthermore, external validation on a real-world dataset of N = 803 resolved binary questions (ForecastBench), forecast by a committee of five LLM personas, shows that the DURO operator reduces Brier error by 16.3% relative to the industry-standard Extremized Average. Together these validate DSP-C as a base-rate-free decomposition-and-calibration engine for subjective belief, and demonstrate that the same machinery extends to multi-agent AI workflows as a guardrail against hallucinatory guessing.

detail.abstract: Self-improving intelligent systems can revise prompts, accumulate skills, adapt model parameters, and optimize computational infrastructure. Their gains do not necessarily accumulate or benefit the systems in which they operate. Retained experience can lose applicability, interacting updates can create regressions, and excessive protection of historical behavior can obstruct useful adaptation. This integrative review connects historical work on learning machines, case reuse, adaptive software, regression testing, and continual learning with contemporary research on language agents, verification, robotics, and computational co-design. It organizes the literature by the object of adaptation, the persistence of change, and the boundary at which improvement is evaluated. The synthesis motivates Embedded Self-Improvement (ESI), a proposed framework centered on dependency-conditioned intervention memory: records that connect changes to observed effects, applicability conditions, interactions, and revalidation requirements. ESI separates further exploration from deployment, and retention of evidence from preservation of capability. The article specifies a reference procedure, an illustrative update lifecycle, and a prospective evaluation design that measures cumulative verified gain at a fixed evaluation budget under explicit harm and retention limits. Its candidate contribution lies in coupling intervention history to test selection and evidence invalidation across repeated updates. The review identifies competing methods, conditions under which this coupling may fail, and research directions for algorithms, models, and products. Its value remains an empirical question rather than an established advantage.

detail.abstract: We study stochastic dynamic resource allocation with continuously distributed rewards. Together, these results sharpen our understanding of CE and establish its near-optimality for dynamic resource allocation problems across a substantially broader class of stochastic models.

detail.abstract:
Agricultural technology increasingly makes temperature, humidity, light, irrigation, carbon dioxide, airflow, and other production variables technically controllable. Yet technical controllability is not the same as economic desirability. Each additional layer of control can raise yield, quality, timing reliability, or loss avoidance while also adding capital, energy, maintenance, sensing, integration, and management costs. This paper develops the Profitable Control framework by formalizing the argument in Kao (2026a) that the relevant question is not whether a variable can be controlled, but whether it is worth paying to control. The framework treats control as an economic choice over intensity rather than a binary technological capability.

The paper connects greenhouse optimal-control research, controlled-environment agriculture, vertical-farming economics, techno-economic benchmarking, and recent work on AI-enabled climate control. Existing studies already optimize yield, energy use, profit, and resource efficiency within particular systems. The contribution here is integrative rather than a claim to a new control-theoretic method: it introduces a portable vocabulary for comparing control decisions across crops, technologies, and locations. Four concepts organize the framework: Control Value, Control Burden, Profitable Control, and the Economic Control Boundary. A lightweight formulation states that tighter control is justified only when its expected incremental economic value exceeds its full incremental control burden.

Recent evidence illustrates why this distinction matters. Autonomous greenhouse systems can choose among very different lighting, heating, carbon-dioxide, irrigation, and harvest strategies while being judged on profit rather than biological output alone. Model-predictive control can materially reduce energy use and improve economic performance without necessarily making an otherwise unattractive production system viable. Vertical-farm studies likewise show that optimal settings depend on electricity prices, climate, crop physiology, capital structure, and the value of the crop being sold. The central implication is that AI does not repeal the economics of physical control. Its value lies in shifting the cost-value relationship of control: using existing equipment more selectively, responding to changing prices and crop states, and concentrating precision where the crop can pay for it.

detail.abstract:
Black-Scholes pricing assumes volatility is a single value, but the market does not provide one. Each option has a bid implied volatility and an ask implied volatility, and the spread varies over time. This project prices SPX index options by considering this disparity. Volatility is modeled as a triangular fuzzy number based on observed bid and ask implied volatilities, the fuzziness is propagated through the Black-Scholes formula using α-cut arithmetic, and the fuzzy parameters are conditioned on hidden market regimes inferred by a Gaussian Hidden Markov Model fitted to S&P 500 returns. The result is a regime-aware price band whose adequacy is tested against realized market quotes using Kupiec unconditional coverage and Christoffersen independence tests. 

Out of sample across three walk-forward folds spanning 2019-2026, the pre-registered construction, with supports anchored to the bid-ask spread, fails nominal coverage by roughly an order of magnitude at every level tested. A diagnosed and corrected construction, using training-window deviation quantiles in place of bid-ask gaps, closes most of this gap at the cost of substantially wider bands. A further decomposition finds that pooled coverage statistics can conceal exactly where regime-conditioning matters: a pooled, unconditional band shows little advantage from conditioning on average, but stratified by market regime, conditioning closes coverage gaps of up to 68 percentage points specifically in stressed markets.

The model is derived from fifteen years of participation in Members Church of God International (MCGI) and subsequent documentary research. It links Weberian routinization to three economic processes: rising legitimacy costs after charismatic succession, the displacement of operating costs onto members and households, and the growing detachability of media, property, brands, and commercial ventures from the congregation that financed their development.

The model identifies Moral Inflation as declining reputational return to repeated public good works, the Zero-Cost Ledger as the transfer of labor and operating costs outside formal organizational accounts, and the Two Clocks as the asymmetry between irreversible human time and a revisable institutional horizon. These processes converge at the Disposal Threshold, where adjacent assets can retain value, labor, customers, financing, or demand even as congregational subsidy shrinks. MCGI supplies the theory-generating case, with Hillsong and the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification used as mechanism comparators.

This essay examines the "crabs in a barrel" metaphor and the assumptions it carries about competition, solidarity, and advancement within marginalized groups. Drawing on research on Crabs in the Barrel Syndrome, social identity, social comparison, tokenism, relative deprivation, and internalized oppression, it considers why people who share group membership sometimes withhold support, gatekeep opportunity, or experience one another's advancement as a threat. 

The essay argues that focusing exclusively on individual behavior obscures the organizational conditions in which that behavior occurs, including real and perceived scarcity, constrained mobility, politicized climates, and unequal access to development and power. Examining the barrel does not excuse harmful conduct or eliminate individual agency. detail.abstract: Monetary gifting at weddings and other life-cycle celebrations is often narrated through a practical rule of thumb: "covering the plate." This paper argues that the contemporary cash envelope is better understood as a cultural accounting device that translates belonging, obligation, and relational continuity into a standardized, comparable amount. Using a structured survey of celebration attendees in Israel, where cash is the dominant gift medium, we examine how givers convert social meaning into numbers, and how norms, relationships, and household budgeting jointly shape monetary gifts. The data reveal a coherent set of patterns. Giving is anchored to perceived hosting costs, yet typically exceeds them: the median gift-to-plate ratio is approximately 1.30, consistent with "support beyond reimbursement" rather than simple cost-matching. Generosity is also calibrated to the household or attending party rather than to the individual guest, since the total envelope scales sublinearly with party size, with an elasticity near 0.50, so that doubling the party raises the total gift by only about 41% and produces a mechanical decline in gifts per person. This party-size compression holds across the distribution but weakens among the most generous givers, pointing to a mix of budgeting and more expressive giving. The plate-cost anchor is itself relationship-dependent, predicting per-person gifts far more strongly among close family than among weak ties such as coworkers, where giving is more standardized. Finally, cash is institutionalized unevenly across event types, dominating weddings far more than other celebrations. We interpret these results through classic theories of gift exchange and obligation (Mauss, 1990), the social marking of money (Zelizer, 1989), and embeddedness in relational structures (Granovetter, 1985; Polanyi, 2001). The envelope thus functions less like a price and more like a ledger entry in a modern ritual economy, a way of quantifying belonging without fully submitting it to the market.

In a cross-market transaction, a right may attach to one shareholder market but not another, exist legally but be unusable through the ordinary custody channel, or deliver cash rather than the spun-off security. This paper asks not only whether a safeguard exists, but on whom it is conferred and whether it can be exercised in practice. It develops a five-dimension coding framework-coverage, exercisability, delivery, shareholder voice and market channel-and applies it to a source-linked registry of Hong Kong-listed parent-SpinCo transactions. Midea-Annto and Weichai-Lovol illustrate A/H legal-eligibility asymmetry; WH-Smithfield and Sihuan-Xuanzhu illustrate infrastructure constraints. Completed distributions provide comparison cases. The evidence supports mechanism and existence claims, not population frequencies or causal effects. A procedural benchmark asks whether differential treatment is justified, disclosed, practicable, and accompanied by a security route, monetised substitute or reasoned explanation. The contribution is to recast investor protection as a question of rights incidence and institutional capacity rather than rule presence alone.

title: Efficiency without Forgetting: A Structured Review of Redundancy-aware, Resource-efficient and Few-shot Continual Adaptation of Vision-language Models

detail.title: Efficiency without Forgetting: A Structured Review of Redundancy-aware, Resource-efficient and Few-shot Continual Adaptation of Vision-language Models

detail.abstract: Vision-language models such as CLIP place images and text in a shared embedding space and classify categories they were never trained on. Keeping such a model useful after deployment requires repeated adaptation, and three constraints then act at once: previously acquired knowledge degrades, including the zero-shot ability that was never learned as a task; each update consumes computation, memory, time and energy; and the examples available for a new concept are often few. A fourth constraint is analysed less often and cuts across the other three: redundancy, meaning parameters, modules, stored samples, computation, representation directions or ranks that are trained, kept or recomputed without measurable benefit. This review examines 42 primary studies on continual adaptation of pre-trained vision-language models, published between 2022 and September 2026 and identified through a documented and auditable search-and-coding protocol, together with 15 adjacent studies that supply efficiency or redundancy evidence from outside this setting. Studies are classified by a single mechanism axis into five families and coded along six cross-cutting dimensions, among them a six-way distinction between types of redundancy. Three findings are supported by the coded evidence. Reporting of resource cost is one-sided: trainable-parameter counts appear for 19 of the 42 primary studies, peak memory for five, wall-clock time for six, and energy for none, so claims of frugality rest on a quantity that does not determine the others. Parameter-minimal design and explicit redundancy control, which occupied separate lines of work until 2024, now appear together in methods that minimise trainable rank, share low-rank factors across tasks or compose sparse expert updates. Individual methods nonetheless quantify redundancy only through diagnostics internal to themselves, and no standardized redundancy metric is used consistently across this literature, which is why the field has gained redundancy-aware methods without gaining a way to rank them. Heterogeneous protocols, backbones, task orders and shot counts further make most cross-paper numerical comparisons invalid; the defensible comparisons come from tables inside single papers. The review states what the evidence supports, marks what it does not, and identifies the remaining gaps, of which standardized redundancy measurement and resource-normalised evaluation are the most consequential.

detail.abstract:
Purpose: This paper develops an integrated four-layer empirical monitoring framework for diagnosing multi-asset systemic stress, positioned within the empirical systemic-risk tradition of Kritzman et al. (2011) and Diebold and Yilmaz (2014) rather than as a structural equilibrium asset-pricing model. The objective is to provide institutional risk managers and macro analysts with a reproducible diagnostic architecture combining network topology, dynamic causality analysis, tail-risk quantification, and regime classification, applied concurrently with an active stress event. The paper does not aim to forecast returns, identify the stochastic discount factor, or test market efficiency.

Design/methodology/approach: Four methodological layers are integrated: network topology via Mantegna (1999) correlation distance, multidimensional scaling, Ward clustering, and minimum spanning trees; dynamic causality via pairwise Granger testing with Bonferroni correction, lead-lag cross-correlation, and joint F-tests in a nine-asset VAR; tail risk via Conditional Value-at-Risk and Longin and Solnik (2001) tail dependence; regime classification via the Kritzman et al. (2011) Absorption Ratio and a hidden Markov model with BIC selection and out-of-sample evaluation. Analysis covers nine global asset classes from April 2025 to April 2026 (N = 261), supplemented by a 14-year long-history sample (N = 3,472).

Findings: The Absorption Ratio 0.50 threshold (Kritzman et al., 2011) is breached in all four crisis windows tested (the Global Financial Crisis, COVID-19, the 2022–2023 Federal Reserve tightening cycle, and the current-study window), providing multi-episode threshold validation. Bonferroni correction reduces 15 uncorrected Granger relationships to 4, all pointing to Japan Equity. The DCC-GARCH minimum spanning tree converges with the Granger evidence on Japan Equity centrality. The out-of-sample hidden Markov model, trained on 14 years of multi-crisis data and applied without re-estimation, correctly identifies the April 2026 stress regime. Joint F-tests support Oil quasi-exogeneity in conditional mean while variance decomposition reveals volatility-channel transmission to equities and rates.

Research limitations/implications: The 261-observation current-study window is short for systemic-risk modelling; conclusions specific to this window are exploratory. The multi-crisis Absorption Ratio replication, long-history DCC-GARCH baseline, and out-of-sample hidden Markov model evaluation mitigate but do not eliminate single-episode concerns. Granger findings are subject to heteroskedasticity, non-linear dependence, and finite-sample size distortions; only Bonferroni-surviving results are treated as robust. The framework provides no equilibrium interpretation. Future research should pursue walk-forward hidden Markov model evaluation on larger samples, asymmetric and block DCC specifications, Student-t and copula-based tail dependence extensions, and transfer-entropy or non-linear Granger frameworks for non-linear predictability structures.

Practical implications: The framework offers institutional risk managers a reproducible monitoring architecture combining four methodologically independent diagnostics. Portfolio managers obtain a multi-method check on diversification assumptions during stress periods. The volume-weighted minimum spanning tree provides a capital-commitment-aware view of cross-asset structure that complements the price-correlation view. The out-of-sample hidden Markov model enables real-time regime classification using only historical data. Risk officers receive defensible directional findings (Bonferroni-corrected Granger) that survive the most stringent multiple-testing correction. Macro strategists gain a transparent map of which assets transmit shocks through mean predictability versus through volatility-channel effects on forecast-error variance.

Social implications: Open and reproducible systemic-risk monitoring tools support broader financial-stability objectives valued by regulators, central banks, and institutional fiduciaries who serve household savers, pension beneficiaries, and insurance policyholders. The framework's open-source code and fully bundled data pipeline lower the methodological barrier for smaller institutions, academic researchers in emerging markets, and graduate students who may lack access to proprietary risk platforms. By providing methodologically triangulated diagnostics rather than single-method signals, the framework helps reduce overconfidence in any one indicator, a recurring contributor to retail and institutional losses during prior systemic crises.

detail.abstract: Over-the-counter (OTC) Spot Contract-for-Difference (CFD) retail and institutional liquidity pools suffer from structural opacity, as broker-specific tick volumes fail to capture centralized limit order book (LOB) depth where primary price discovery occurs. This paper presents a cross-venue microstructure telemetry architecture that bridges centralized exchange Level-2 order books-specifically CME Globex Futures (GC , SI , CL , ES , NQ , YM) and Binance Spot/Perpetual Level-2 DOM-directly into an automated MT5 ECN execution engine. We formulate a real-time rolling futures-to-spot basis adjustment () that projects institutional limit-order clusters ("Whale Bid/Ask Walls") onto spot CFD charts with sub-second latency. Furthermore, we construct a multi-level Order Book Imbalance () veto gate that blocks spot entries whenever centralized limit liquidity opposes the short-term momentum signal (e.g., during a short trigger or proximity within of an unabsorbed CME whale wall). Live empirical execution data across Gold (XAUUSD), Crude Oil (USOIL), and Ethereum (ETHUSD) confirms that cross-venue LOB gating prevents institutional absorption losses during post-session liquidity thinning.

title: A Quarter-Point With Global Consequences

detail.abstract: The Federal Reserve's decision on September 16, 2026, to raise the federal funds target range by 0.25 percentage point, to 3.75%-4.00%, is modest in arithmetic but consequential in meaning. It is the first increase since July 2023 and reverses the direction of the Fed's most recent policy adjustment. The vote was unanimous. More important, the September projections show a median year-end policy rate of 4.1%, consistent with one additional quarterpoint increase before the end of 2026. The Fed is therefore not merely fine-tuning overnight rates. It is telling households, companies, markets, foreign governments, and the White House that persistent inflation now outweighs the case for easier money. The decision arrives in an unusually difficult setting. U.S. demand and investment remain resilient, unemployment is low, and the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) projects 2.3% real growth in 2026. Yet personal consumption expenditures inflation is projected at 3.7%, far above the 2% objective. A Middle East conflict and disrupted energy flows have lifted oil prices, while tariffs and an artificial-intelligence investment boom add other supply and demand pressures. A rate increase cannot reopen an oil pipeline or create electricity capacity. It can, however, limit the chance that an initial energy-price shock spreads into wages, services, rents, contracts, and long-term inflation expectations. At home, the burden will be uneven. Variable-rate borrowers, credit-card users, small firms, prospective homebuyers, commercial-property owners, and companies facing near-term refinancing will feel the tightening first. Existing fixed-rate borrowers are largely insulated, while savers may earn more if banks pass the increase through to deposit rates. The policy's broader effects on hiring, capital spending, and inflation will take months. Today's market signal may matter more immediately than the 25 basis points themselves: investors now have to price a central bank willing to tighten again despite political pressure and despite the risk that higher rates reinforce the growth damage from expensive energy.

detail.abstract: Empirical work on instant-runoff voting (IRV) currently reports axiomatic failures, monotonicity reversals, Condorcet-winner elimination, participation ("no-show") paradoxes, independenceof-irrelevant-alternatives (IIA) violations, as binary events: did a given real or simulated election exhibit the failure, yes or no. Under this framing, the dominant empirical finding in the literature (Ornstein & Norman, 2014; Miller, 2017; Graham-Squire & McCune, 2023; Fox & Bruyns, 2025) is that such failures are rare in real elections. A binary indicator discards exactly the information needed to judge how much confidence that rarity finding deserves: an election that narrowly avoided a reversal and one that avoided it by a landslide are coded identically. We define, for a cast ballot profile and each of the four axioms above, a margin: the minimum number of ballot edits of a specified, axiom-respecting type needed to flip the election outcome. This version of the document carries the full theoretical development: we prove an exact, round-local characterization of the monotonicity margin (correcting an imprecision in the natural first guess at the relevant gap quantity, and converting what was previously only a conjecture about its tightness into a proved theorem for fixed candidate count); we prove matching zero-detection, deficit-based lower bound, and NP-hardness results for the Condorcet-elimination margin, together with a greedy O(log m)-approximation; we prove a two-mechanism lower bound for the participation margin that accounts for the shrinking majority denominator under withdrawal, and explain why exact computation is combinatorially hard; we prove exact tractability for the IIA margin under full candidate removal and a matching lower bound under partial truncation; and we replace the originally conjectured probabilistic duality between the monotonicity margin and strategic manipulability with a theorem that is true rather than merely plausible: both quantities are governed by the same family of round-local vote gaps, which is a weaker but provable statement than the one originally proposed. We close with a complete, precise specification of the simulation and empirical study that will instantiate and test these definitions in code.

detail.abstract: Using Chinese A-share stocks eligible for margin trading and short selling from 2010 to 2025, this study constructs measures of margin-financing and short-selling activity along three dimensions: changes in outstanding balances, relative trading intensity, and sentiment momentum. Principal component analysis is then used to construct a composite factor capturing the relative strength of margin financing versus short selling. The factor significantly predicts lower future stock returns. A long-short portfolio that is long low-factor stocks and short high-factor stocks earns significant positive returns at both daily and weekly frequencies, and the predictive relation remains robust after controlling for conventional risk factors and firm characteristics. Predictive power declines as the holding horizon lengthens. Return predictability is stronger when investor sentiment is more intense or optimistic and among stocks with stronger lottery-like characteristics, consistent with short-term mispricing and subsequent price correction. The main findings remain robust after accounting for transaction costs, factor orthogonalization, and separate tests in bull and bear markets.

detail.abstract: India is fighting a fraud its law has not yet learnt to name. A caller announces himself as a police officer, the CBI or the Enforcement Directorate, sometimes in uniform on video, with a forged warrant on screen. What follows is a custody unknown to the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita: a "digital arrest", in which the person called is kept on camera for hours or days, forbidden to speak to family, and persuaded to move his savings into accounts described as being under judicial custody. He is not robbed; he is frightened into paying, and by the time the fear lifts the money has travelled through a chain of mule accounts and left the banking system. The question the law has still not answered is who then carries the loss: the depositor who authorised the transfer under terror, the bank that executed it without a second look, the platform that carried the call, or nobody at all. At present, by default and by silence, the victim does. This paper argues that the default is neither just nor inevitable, and survives only because Indian law has misclassified the problem. The Reserve Bank's customer-protection regime is built around the unauthorised transaction, whereas digital-arrest fraud is authorised by a deceived customer and falls outside it; India has built impressive interdiction machinery, but interdiction is not allocation. In Re: Victims of Digital Arrest, the Supreme Court has asked a committee to design a shared-liability framework that does not exist. Drawing on comparative loss-allocation theory and the cheapest cost avoider, this paper supplies the fault-based, multi-actor model that framework lacks. The Reserve Bank's first response to the Court, a draft Standard Operating Procedure of September 2026, governs the freezing of suspected mule accounts and says nothing about who bears the loss.

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the local economic impact of grassroots, community-organized sports events. We utilize the Village Basketball Association and Village Super League in Guizhou, China, as a natural experiment to identify causal effects on host-county economic activity. We construct a quarterly panel of 16 counties from 2022 to 2025 and deploy a staggered difference-indifferences strategy. The results show that these events generate a statistically significant 7% increase in tertiary-sector value-added, and the effects accumulate over time as local service capacity expands. We also find a notable divergence. While overall service-sector activity increases, there is no measurable effect on retail sales. We argue that this divergence is consistent with China's statistical reporting thresholds, which exclude many of the small businesses and informal e-commerce channels that drive grassroots tourism. Overall, the findings suggest that grassroots events built on existing public infrastructure can generate local economic effects that differ from common patterns in the professional sports literature. These results point to the importance of supporting local cultural assets and expanding digital reach in underdeveloped regions.

detail.abstract: The Correction Freeze Problem (CFP) describes four independent ways in which a corrective mechanism can fail to fire. The Error Correction Model (ECM), together with its threshold and band variants (TVECM and BVECM), is the standard econometric tool for measuring correction. This paper proposes a formal link between the two. We argue that the ECM gives CFP's abstract update rule an estimable form: a negative adjustment coefficient 𝛼 marks successful correction, and CFP supplies conditions under which 𝛼 could fall to zero within a regime. The TVECM and BVECM then correspond to CFP's threshold and cost mechanisms. We take Mekong River sediment starvation as a promising first case in which the threshold parameter 𝛾 might be estimated from obtainable data, and we lay out an estimation protocol built on Mekong River Commission monitoring records, dam construction dates and published sediment load series. The paper reports no estimates. It closes with a general estimation strategy and a list of open issues, chiefly how CFP's threshold on increments relates to the TVECM threshold on levels, and which series should play the part of the perceived state.

detail.abstract:
Purpose: This paper presents the Cost-Schedule Escalation Spiral Theory (CSEST), a mid-range theory explaining why cost overruns and schedule delays on construction projects behave as a mutually reinforcing process rather than two independent failures, why recovery interventions can paradoxically worsen the condition they are meant to correct, and why deterioration can persist after its triggering disturbance is resolved. 

Design/methodology/approach: CSEST's constructs and propositions were developed through formal theory-construction work, then adjudicated against the literature through a systematic review of ten adjacent theoretical traditions using a five-category scheme (retain, refine, merge, reject, unresolved). Descriptive case material from the author's ongoing, unpublished book research was used only as source content for the theory's mechanism vocabulary, flagged as such throughout. 

Findings: CSEST specifies eleven constructs, a four-state project trajectory (Stable, Strained, Spiralling, Entrenched), four feedback loops, and seven propositions addressing reciprocal influence, a threshold transition, a recovery paradox, mediation and moderation through complexity and resource erosion, and contextual amplification by institutional friction and economic volatility. No existing theory offers an equivalent integrated account; Conservation of Resources theory is the closest analogue. 

Research limitations/implications: CSEST is empirically unvalidated; several constructs lack validated instruments, and the review was single-reviewer and English-language only. 

Practical implications: The theory yields observable early-warning indicators and a composite Spiral Index for project monitoring. 

Social implications: Reducing escalation-driven overruns conserves scarce infrastructure investment, benefiting the communities such projects serve. 

Originality/value: CSEST is the first mid-range theory to integrate reciprocal cost-schedule feedback, threshold dynamics, mediated recovery and contextual amplification in one testable framework.

detail.abstract: Values-based leadership is often described in terms of integrity, compassion, authenticity, and responsibility, yet values become meaningful through the decisions leaders make under pressure. This mixed methods study examined whether self-reported inclusive leadership behaviour was associated with leaders' perceived ability to recover from stress, and how leaders described applying values in practice. Thirty-one adults with leadership or supervisory experience completed the nine-item Inclusive Leadership Scale, the six-item Brief Resilience Scale, and three open-ended questions. Inclusive leadership and resilience were positively associated, r(29) = .62, p < .001, 95% CI [.34, .80]. A simple regression accounted for 38.1% of the observed variance in resilience. Thematic analysis identified six patterns: integrity under pressure; compassion and dignity; authenticity and role modelling; inclusion and psychological safety; tensions between values; and learning across contexts. Participants described values as practical guides to decisions, especially when fairness, accountability, or care competed with operational demands. The study did not measure employee engagement or establish a causal effect of leadership on resilience. Its contribution is a preliminary association alongside accounts of how leaders try to put values into action.

Its growing scope across model developers, application developers, and deployers increases the practical importance of a second question: how can an institution translate HAIP reporting expectations into internal controls, assignable responsibilities, reusable evidence, and continuing review without treating distinct governance frameworks as equivalent? This working paper develops an institution-level implementation crosswalk for that purpose. The paper distinguishes three layers of interoperability-semantic, control, and evidence interoperability-and proposes a Reporting-to-Implementation Chain linking an external governance expectation to an institutional control objective, accountable owner, operating procedure, evidence artifact, review mechanism, and update trigger. title: Aided Rationality and Technology-Augmented Decision-Making: A Randomized Controlled Experiment

detail.title: Aided Rationality and Technology-Augmented Decision-Making: A Randomized Controlled Experiment

detail.abstract:
The emergence of generative AI as an everyday decision-support tool raises a fundamental question for behavioral economics: can access to AI-powered information assistance move individual decision-making systematically closer to the rational choice benchmark, and under what conditions does it do so? This paper introduces and empirically tests the concept of aided rationality — an intermediate cognitive state between Simon's (1972) bounded rationality and the classical ideal of full rationality, achieved when individuals augment their judgment with AI-generated informational signals. We formalize aided rationality through a structural model in which each agent's information state θᵢ ∈ [0,1] is shifted upward by AI assistance according to Δθᵢ = δ · αᵢ · g(λᵢ), where δ denotes AI signal precision, αᵢ captures cognitive ability, and λᵢ is an individual-level algorithm trust parameter. The model's central theoretical result — the Inverted-U Trust Hypothesis — states that rationality gains from AI assistance follow a non-monotone inverted-U relationship with algorithm trust, parameterized by the trust-response function g(λ) = 4λ(1−λ). Agents at either extreme — those who distrust AI entirely and those who defer to it unconditionally. This prediction is non-obvious, distinguishes the framework from prior work on algorithm aversion (Dietvorst et al., 2015) and algorithm appreciation (Logg et al., 2019), and has not been previously tested.

We test the model's five pre-specified hypotheses using a pre-registered three-arm between-subject randomized controlled experiment. Participants are randomly assigned to a Control arm (no technological assistance, devices physically collected), a Search-Aided arm (passive search tools permitted, generative AI blocked), or a GenAI-Aided arm (ChatGPT, Gemini, and equivalent tools freely available).

The primary outcome is the Decision Quality Score (DQS), a pre-specified count of expected-value-maximizing choices across eight decision tasks spanning canonical behavioral biases from the Kahneman-Tversky (1979) tradition: the certainty effect, the common ratio effect, loss aversion, gain-loss framing, Bayesian base-rate neglect, the conjunction fallacy, multi-attribute dominance, and probabilistic insurance. The last task is designated a pre-specified null — the model predicts attenuated AI effects in emotionally loaded insurance domains due to ambiguity aversion that is resistant to informational correction. The primary estimating equation is an OLS regression of standardized DQS on treatment indicators, site fixed effects, and the full vector of pre-treatment covariates. The Inverted-U Trust Hypothesis is tested via a quadratic interaction regression with a pre-specified sign pattern (β₄ > 0, β₅ < 0) and an estimated turning point consistent with λᵢ ≈ 0.5.

Practically, the findings speak to the design of AI-assisted decision environments in consumer finance, public policy, and organizational management, where understanding the conditions under which AI assistance improves rather than distorts judgment is of first-order importance. The study is pre-registered on the AEA RCT Registry with a fully locked pre-analysis plan, including exact regression specifications, variable definitions, and the analysis code to be executed without modification on the collected dataset.

detail.abstract: Public insolvency records often separate collateral proceeds, unsecured deficiencies, reserves and successive distributions across different documents and stages. detail.abstract: This paper argues that AI agents should be developed inside the firm that deploys them, and that the current wave of agent acquisitions is not sustainable. It begins with a review of eleven agent security incidents from 2025 to 2026, including the escape of OpenAI models from an evaluation sandbox to breach Hugging Face and a series of breaches at four AI labs traced to a single outside evaluation vendor. Most incidents occurred where agents crossed organisational boundaries: vendors, plug-ins, packages, or environments the deploying firm did not control. Drawing on transaction cost theory, the resource-based view, and security engineering, the paper develops four propositions on security, safety, regulatory reversibility, and integration, and examines them across fourteen cases involving OpenAI, Meta, Google, Nvidia, and Chinese firms. Whole-product acquisitions collapsed or were reversed, most notably Meta-Manus; the agents that scaled fastest in both the US and China were built internally; and benchmark evidence shows that the same model contains attacks far less well inside another vendor's harness. Internal development also eases downstream deployment and hardware integration. The paper concludes that firms should acquire people, not agent systems.
